prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Los Alamos National Laboratory announced Wednesday it is notifying nearly 2,000 current and former employees and visitors that they may have been exposed to beryllium in the lab and may be at risk of disease. Officials are trying to determine the source of beryllium found at Los Alamos National Laboratory. "Letters went out to all of them today," said Kevin Roark, a spokesman for the New Mexico laboratory. Concern over possible exposure to the hard, gray metal, which is purified for use in nuclear weapons and reactors and also used in bicycle frames and golf clubs,  was first raised last November, when a box containing beryllium was received at the laboratory's short-term storage facility, he said. "The package appeared to have damage or degradation of the packing materials, which prompted us to test the area for additional contamination," he said. Surface contamination was found, but it turned out that the box was not the source, Roark said, adding that the source has not been determined. Since the contaminated area had not been tested for the presence of beryllium since 2001, everyone who has entered the restricted-access area since then is being alerted, he said. "It's just one building at one technical area," Roark said, noting that the laboratory covers 36 square miles and has nearly 10,000 employees. Beryllium is hazardous only when its fine, particulate form is inhaled, he said. It was found on surfaces, not in the air, he said.  Find out more about beryllium » . Roark said the alert was sent because "we think it's the responsible, prudent thing to do to let people know we discovered this contamination and to answer their questions if they have any concern about potential for exposure." There are no reports of sickness and "we don't expect anyone to be ill," he said. The laboratory said about 240 employees and 1,650 visitors were potentially at risk because they visited the contaminated areas. About 2 percent of the exposed employees could become sensitized, a smaller percentage of whom could develop chronic beryllium disease, Roark said. Inhalation of powdered beryllium can result in chronic beryllium disease, which can impair lung function in people who are susceptible. The risk to the visitors would be "extremely low" because of the activities they performed and their short exposure time, Roark said. An operator will be available at the laboratory at 505-665-7233 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mountain Time, Monday through Friday.

**(CNN) —** Los Alamos National Laboratory announced Wednesday that it is notifying nearly 2,000 current and former employees and visitors who may have been exposed to beryllium at the laboratory and may be at risk of developing disease.

Officials are working to determine the source of the beryllium found at the facility.

“Letters went out to all of them today,” said Kevin Roark, a spokesman for the New Mexico laboratory.

Concern about possible exposure to the hard, gray metal—purified for use in nuclear weapons and reactors and also used in bicycle frames and golf clubs—first arose last November, when a box containing beryllium arrived at the laboratory’s short-term storage facility, Roark said.

“The package appeared to have damage or degradation of the packing materials, which prompted us to test the area for additional contamination,” he said.

Surface contamination was detected, but the box was ultimately ruled out as the source, Roark said, adding that the source remains undetermined.

Because the contaminated area had not been tested for beryllium since 2001, everyone who has entered the restricted-access area since then is being notified, he said.

“It’s just one building at one technical area,” Roark said, noting that the laboratory spans 36 square miles and employs nearly 10,000 people.

Beryllium is hazardous only when inhaled in a fine, particulate form, he said. It was found on surfaces, not in the air.

**Find out more about beryllium »**

Roark said the alert was issued because “we think it’s the responsible, prudent thing to do to let people know we discovered this contamination and to answer their questions if they have any concern about potential for exposure.”

There have been no reports of illness, and “we don’t expect anyone to be ill,” he said.

According to the laboratory, approximately 240 employees and 1,650 visitors were potentially at risk because they entered the contaminated areas. About 2 percent of the exposed employees could become sensitized, and a smaller percentage of that group could develop chronic beryllium disease, Roark said.

Inhaling powdered beryllium can cause chronic beryllium disease, which can impair lung function in susceptible individuals.

The risk to visitors would be “extremely low” because of the activities they performed and the brevity of their exposure, Roark said.

An operator will be available at the laboratory at **505-665-7233** from **8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mountain Time, Monday through Friday**.

Los Alamos National Laboratory said Wednesday that it is contacting almost 2,000 present and former workers and visitors who may have encountered beryllium at the facility and could face a risk of illness.

Kevin Roark, a spokesperson for the New Mexico laboratory, said notification letters were mailed Wednesday. Laboratory officials are still investigating where the beryllium contamination originated.

The concern began in November after a container holding beryllium arrived at the laboratory’s temporary storage facility. According to Roark, the package’s wrapping appeared damaged or deteriorated, leading officials to examine the surrounding area for contamination. Tests detected beryllium on surfaces, but investigators later determined that the container was not the source. The actual origin remains unknown.

Because the affected location had not been checked for beryllium since 2001, the laboratory is notifying everyone who has entered that restricted area during the intervening years. Roark emphasized that the contamination was limited to a single building within one technical area. Los Alamos spans 36 square miles and employs nearly 10,000 people.

Beryllium—a hard, gray metal refined for nuclear weapons and reactors and also used in products such as bicycle frames and golf clubs—is dangerous only when inhaled as fine particles, Roark said. The material was detected on surfaces rather than in the air. Additional information about beryllium is available.

Roark said the laboratory issued the warning because informing people about the discovery and responding to concerns about possible exposure was the responsible and cautious course of action. No illnesses have been reported, and officials do not anticipate that anyone will become sick.

The laboratory estimates that approximately 240 employees and 1,650 visitors may have been at risk because they entered the contaminated locations. Roark said roughly 2 percent of the exposed employees could develop sensitivity to beryllium, and an even smaller proportion might contract chronic beryllium disease.

Breathing powdered beryllium can cause chronic beryllium disease, which may reduce lung function in susceptible individuals. Roark described the danger to visitors as “extremely low,” citing the nature of their activities and the brief amount of time they spent in the area.

A laboratory representative can be reached at 505-665-7233 between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Mountain Time, Monday through Friday.

counterfactuals.output:
### Los Alamos lab warns nearly 2,000 people of possible beryllium exposure

**LOS ALAMOS, New Mexico** — Los Alamos National Laboratory is notifying nearly 2,000 current and former employees and visitors that they may have been exposed to beryllium, a toxic metal used in nuclear weapons research and other specialized work.

The notifications do not necessarily mean each person inhaled beryllium or received a harmful dose. Rather, officials identified individuals who may have entered areas where the material was handled or where contamination could have been present.

Beryllium is valued for being lightweight, strong and heat-resistant, but inhaling its dust or fumes can trigger an immune response in some people. Long-term exposure can cause chronic beryllium disease, a serious and potentially disabling lung condition. Symptoms can include coughing, fatigue, shortness of breath and weight loss, though illness may not appear until years after exposure.

The laboratory is expected to provide affected individuals with information about medical testing and follow-up monitoring. Determining whether someone has developed beryllium sensitivity generally requires specialized blood testing and, in some cases, additional evaluation.

Los Alamos, one of the country’s premier nuclear research facilities, is overseen by the US Department of Energy. The notification is likely to renew scrutiny of workplace safety practices at sites where hazardous materials are used.

Officials have not indicated that all those receiving notices were exposed or that the notification reflects a confirmed outbreak of beryllium-related illness.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the discovery of surface beryllium contamination at Los Alamos, including who may be at risk, possible health effects, and statements from laboratory spokesman Kevin Roark.
counterfactuals.output:
Los Alamos National Laboratory reported finding removable beryllium contamination during surface “swipe” sampling in work areas, including locations not normally associated with beryllium operations. The discovery prompted the laboratory to restrict affected spaces, conduct additional sampling and cleaning, and review work histories to determine who might have encountered contaminated dust.

### Who may be at risk
The principal concern is for people who worked in, cleaned, maintained or moved equipment through the affected areas. Employees who disturbed contaminated surfaces—allowing dust to become airborne—would face the greatest potential exposure. Former workers may also need to be considered because beryllium-related illness can emerge years after exposure. There is also a theoretical risk of dust being carried home on clothing, although the finding of surface contamination does not by itself establish that workers or family members received a harmful dose.

The laboratory said the discovery did not indicate an off-site release or a danger to the surrounding public.

### Possible health effects
Beryllium is most hazardous when inhaled. Exposure can cause:

- **Beryllium sensitization**, an immune reaction that may occur even at low exposures.
- **Chronic beryllium disease**, a potentially disabling and sometimes fatal lung disorder that can develop months or decades later.
- **Acute respiratory irritation** after sufficiently high exposure.
- **Skin irritation or sensitization** from contact.
- **Increased lung-cancer risk** from long-term occupational exposure.

A contaminated surface is therefore evidence of a potential exposure pathway, not proof that anyone has become ill.

### Laboratory response and Kevin Roark’s statements
Laboratory spokesman **Kevin Roark** emphasized that the swipe results represented surface contamination and did not necessarily mean workers had inhaled beryllium or exceeded occupational exposure limits. He said Los Alamos was treating the findings conservatively by securing and cleaning the areas, expanding sampling, investigating how the material spread and identifying employees who might need notification or medical evaluation.

Roark also said there was no indication of a risk to the general public and that, at the time of the announcement, the laboratory had not established that the newly discovered contamination had caused any beryllium-related illness.

# Los Alamos Contacts Nearly 1,900 People After Contamination Found in Restricted Area

**LOS ALAMOS, N.M. —** Los Alamos National Laboratory is contacting 240 employees and about 1,650 visitors who entered a restricted-access area since 2001 after contamination involving beryllium, a toxic metal, was identified there.

Laboratory officials are reviewing access records to determine who may have been exposed and are notifying everyone known to have entered the area as a precaution. Being contacted does not necessarily mean a person inhaled beryllium or will develop health problems.

Beryllium is used in nuclear-weapons research and other specialized scientific work. Dust or particles containing the metal can cause an immune reaction in some people, potentially leading to chronic beryllium disease, a serious and sometimes disabling lung condition. Symptoms can take years to appear.

The laboratory is expected to offer affected individuals information about medical evaluation and testing. Such screening can help identify beryllium sensitivity, although a positive sensitivity test does not by itself mean a person has lung disease.

The large number of notifications reflects the long period under review and includes short-term visitors as well as laboratory workers. Officials are investigating how the contamination occurred, how long it may have been present and whether existing controls failed to prevent material from spreading.

The affected area has been restricted while the laboratory assesses the contamination and determines whether additional cleanup, monitoring or workplace-safety measures are needed.

counterfactuals.output:
**Unidentified beryllium source prompts investigation at Los Alamos facility**

**LOS ALAMOS, N.M. —** Los Alamos National Laboratory is investigating how beryllium entered a facility where the toxic metal was not expected to be present, raising questions about possible worker exposure and prompting additional sampling, access controls and medical follow-up.

Laboratory officials said the source of the beryllium had not been identified. Investigators are reviewing the facility’s work history, equipment, materials, ventilation systems and movement of personnel and supplies to determine whether the contamination came from a current operation, legacy material or beryllium-containing dust carried in from another location.

The laboratory said it restricted access to the affected area after the material was detected and began collecting surface and air samples to determine the extent of contamination. Potentially affected employees are being notified, and workers may be referred for occupational-health evaluations under the laboratory’s beryllium-safety program. Cleaning or other work in the area will be conducted using controls intended to prevent dust from becoming airborne.

Beryllium is a lightweight metal used in nuclear, aerospace and scientific applications because of its strength and other specialized properties. Solid pieces generally pose less risk when left undisturbed. The principal hazard occurs when beryllium-containing dust, fumes or particles are inhaled.

Exposure can cause beryllium sensitization, an immune response that may produce no immediate symptoms but can increase the risk of chronic beryllium disease. That disease can inflame and scar the lungs, leading to coughing, fatigue, chest pain, weight loss and shortness of breath. The condition may develop months or years after exposure. Not everyone exposed becomes sensitized or ill, and the presence of beryllium on a surface does not by itself establish that a person received a harmful dose.

Laboratory officials said the response is focused on identifying who entered or worked in the facility, reconstructing possible exposure pathways and determining whether contamination spread beyond the initial area. Medical testing may include a beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test, a blood test used to identify sensitization. Employees with concerns are being advised not to rely solely on the absence of symptoms because beryllium-related illness can have a delayed onset.

Officials have not announced a conclusion about how the beryllium reached the facility or whether any worker has been diagnosed with a beryllium-related condition. The investigation is expected to continue until the laboratory can identify the source, characterize the affected areas and verify that cleanup and controls are effective.

Members of the public seeking information should call **[INSERT VERIFIED PUBLIC CONTACT NUMBER]**. Los Alamos National Laboratory’s general switchboard is **505-667-5061**, but the incident-specific number should be confirmed with the laboratory before publication. Workers should use the occupational-health or employee-assistance contact provided directly by the laboratory.
